learn.hook: In 1820, during a lecture demonstration, Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire. Electricity and magnetism were joined for good.
points: Oersted's discovery (1820): a current in a straight wire deflects a nearby compass needle. The needle sets along circles around the wire.
Moving charges (currents) produce magnetic fields. Reversing the current reverses the deflection.
Later, Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism and showed light is an electromagnetic wave.
Notation: a dot ⊙ means a field or current coming out of the page (towards you); a cross ⊗ means going into the page.
Magnetic fields obey superposition: the field of several sources is the vector sum of their individual fields. Like E, B is a vector field.

example.q: A compass is placed just below a wire running north-south. When the current flows north, the needle's north pole swings west. What happens if the current is reversed?
steps: Below a wire carrying current northwards, the field points west (right-hand thumb rule), so the north pole swings west.
Reversing the current reverses the field around the wire.
The force on the needle's poles reverses, so it swings the other way.
example.answer: The north pole now swings east

learn.reallife: Railway engineers keep sensitive magnetic compasses and instruments away from heavy-current traction cables on electrified Indian Railways routes, because the current's magnetic field can deflect them.

games.title: Oersted's lessons
items: A steady current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it.
That was Oersted's observation.
A stationary charge produces a magnetic field.
Only moving charges (currents) do.
The symbol ⊗ means a field directed into the page.
Think of the tail feathers of an arrow going away.
Magnetic fields from two sources add as vectors.
Superposition holds for B.
Reversing the current leaves the compass deflection unchanged.
The deflection reverses.

quiz.q: Who first observed that an electric current deflects a magnetic compass needle?
quiz.explain: Oersted noticed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.
quiz.mistake: Credits Faraday, who later discovered induction

quiz.q: In a diagram, a magnetic field pointing straight towards the reader is shown by
quiz.explain: A dot is like the tip of an arrow coming at you.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the dot and cross conventions

quiz.q: A compass placed near a straight wire with current tends to align
options: along circles centred on the wire
quiz.explain: The field of a straight wire forms concentric circles around it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field is along the wire

quiz.q: Which of these produces a magnetic field?
options: A charged comb kept on a table
A neutral atom at rest with no magnetic moment
quiz.explain: Moving charges make magnetic fields; static charges make only electric fields.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any charge makes a magnetic field

quiz.q: Two wires each produce a field of 3 µT at a point, in the same direction. What is the net field there (in µT)?
quiz.explain: Superposition: same direction, so the fields add: 3 + 3 = 6 µT.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the fields cancel

quiz.q: Two wires produce fields of 3 µT (east) and 4 µT (north) at a point. What is the magnitude of the net field (in µT)?
quiz.mistake: Adds magnitudes directly

quiz.q: Maxwell's work showed that
options: electricity and magnetism are unified, and light is an electromagnetic wave
currents do not produce magnetic fields
light is a stream of electrons
quiz.explain: Maxwell's equations predicted EM waves moving at the speed of light.
quiz.mistake: Credits Maxwell with Oersted's discovery

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A compass needle deflects near a wire only while current flows. Reason (R): Only moving charges produce magnetic fields. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: When the current stops, the charges no longer drift, so there is no magnetic field to turn the needle.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the field to the motion of charges

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my compass go crazy near a wire with current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Moving charges in the wire make a magnetic field around it, which turns the compass. Thanks, Oersted!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a current produce around it?

topics.title: Lorentz force on a moving charge

learn.hook: Charged particles from the Sun are steered by Earth's magnetic field into the polar skies, painting the auroras. The steering force is the Lorentz force.
points: Lorentz force: F = q[E + v × B]. The magnetic part is F = q(v × B), magnitude qvB sinθ.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both v and B. It is zero if the charge is at rest or moves along B (θ = 0 or 180°).
Direction: use the right-hand rule for v × B (fingers along v, curl towards B, thumb gives the force on a positive charge). Reverse it for a negative charge.
SI unit of B: tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹. Smaller unit: gauss, 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T.
Typical fields: Earth's surface about 10⁻⁵ T; a lab magnet about 1 T; a neutron star about 10⁸ T.

example.q: A proton moves at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. Find the force on it.
example.answer: 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N, perpendicular to both v and B

learn.reallife: Auroras are rarely seen from India, but ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory studies the solar wind whose charged particles feel the Lorentz force as they reach Earth's magnetic field.

games.title: Lorentz force check
items: The magnetic force on a charge at rest is zero.
v = 0 means qv × B = 0.
A charge moving parallel to B feels the maximum magnetic force.
sin 0° = 0, so the force is zero.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity.
It comes from a cross product with v.
1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ tesla.
So Earth's ~0.5 G field is ~5 × 10⁻⁵ T.
An electron and a proton moving the same way in the same field feel forces in the same direction.
Opposite charges get opposite forces.

quiz.q: An electron moves at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a field of 0.2 T. What is the magnitude of the force on it (in units of 10⁻¹⁴ N)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: A charge of 2 µC moves at 10⁴ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a field of 0.5 T. What is the magnetic force (in mN)?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°

quiz.q: A proton moves along +x in a field along +y. What is the direction of the magnetic force on it?
quiz.mistake: Uses the left-hand order or forgets the cross product

quiz.q: An electron moves along +x in a field along +y. The magnetic force on it points along
quiz.explain: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, and the negative charge flips it to -z.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reverse the direction for a negative charge

quiz.q: A charged particle moves through a region with no deflection. Which conclusion is certain?
options: It cannot be concluded that B = 0, since the particle may be moving along B
The particle must be at rest
quiz.explain: A charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force, so the field could be non-zero.
quiz.mistake: Assumes no deflection always means no field

quiz.q: Why does the magnetic force not change the speed of a charge?
options: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
It acts only on charges at rest
It is parallel to the velocity
quiz.explain: A force perpendicular to motion changes direction but not kinetic energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any force must change the speed

quiz.q: Which is the SI unit of magnetic field?
quiz.explain: The tesla (T) is the SI unit; the gauss is a smaller non-SI unit.
quiz.mistake: Confuses field (T) with flux (Wb)

quiz.q: The Lorentz force on a charge q in combined fields is
quiz.explain: Electric force qE plus magnetic force q(v × B).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which field the velocity multiplies

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a magnetic field pushes a moving charge, why doesn't the charge speed up?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It only turns the charge!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the angle between the magnetic force and the velocity?

learn.hook: Every electric motor, from a ceiling fan to an electric scooter, works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field gets a push.
points: A straight conductor of length l carrying current I in a uniform field B feels F = I l × B, magnitude BIl sinθ.
This is just the sum of Lorentz forces on the drifting electrons in the wire.
Direction: l points along the current; use the right-hand rule (or Fleming's left-hand rule).
A horizontal wire can float if the magnetic force balances its weight: BIl = mg.
On individual charges, the magnetic force does no work, so their speed stays constant.

example.q: A 0.2 m wire of mass 20 g lies horizontally in a horizontal field of 0.5 T perpendicular to it. What current makes it float? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)

learn.reallife: Loudspeakers in a Bollywood cinema hall use a coil in a magnet's field. The force BIl on the coil changes with the audio current and moves the speaker cone.

items.q: Wire parallel to B: F (in N)

games.title: Force on wires
items: The force on a current-carrying wire is maximum when it is perpendicular to B.
The force on a wire is along the direction of the current.
It is perpendicular to both the wire and B.
Doubling the current doubles the force on the wire.
F ∝ I.
The magnetic force on moving electrons changes their speed.
It does no work on them.
A wire carrying current parallel to B feels no force.

quiz.q: A wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.3 T. What force acts on it (in N)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets one of the factors

quiz.q: A 10 cm wire carries 5 A at 30° to a 0.8 T field. What is the force on it (in N)?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30°

quiz.q: A horizontal rod of mass 0.1 kg and length 0.5 m is suspended in a horizontal field of 0.49 T perpendicular to it. What current makes the tension in the support threads zero (in A)? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses mass instead of weight

quiz.q: A horizontal wire carries current towards the north in a magnetic field pointing vertically upward. In which direction is the force on the wire?
quiz.explain: F = I l × B. Taking x = east, y = north and z = up: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so the force points east.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the cross product and gets west

quiz.q: Why does a magnetic field do no work on the charges in a wire, even though the wire itself can be pushed?
options: Work is done only on protons
The force on each charge is perpendicular to its velocity
quiz.explain: Each charge's magnetic force is perpendicular to its motion, so no work is done on it directly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the magnetic field directly supplies the energy

quiz.q: The force on a straight conductor in a uniform field is given by
quiz.explain: F = I l × B, with l along the current.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cross product or uses a dot product

quiz.q: The current in a wire is doubled and the field is halved. The force on the wire
quiz.mistake: Changes only one factor

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A current-carrying wire placed along a magnetic field feels no force. Reason (R): The force on a wire is BIl sinθ, and θ = 0 here. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin 0° = 0, so the force vanishes when the wire is parallel to B.
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the sinθ factor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a motor get its push from a magnet?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels F = BIl sinθ, which pushes the coil round. Vroom!
teach.nudge: Good! What force acts on a wire carrying current in a magnetic field?

topics.title: Circular and helical motion in a magnetic field

learn.hook: Particle accelerators and mass spectrometers bend charged particles into circles with magnets. The radius tells you the particle's momentum.
points: A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B moves in a circle: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB).
Angular frequency ω = qB/m; frequency ν = qB/(2πm); period T = 2πm/(qB). These do not depend on speed or radius (cyclotron frequency).
If v has a component v∥ along B, that part is unaffected, while v⊥ makes the circle: the path is a helix.
Pitch of the helix = distance moved along B in one revolution = v∥T = 2πm v∥/(qB). Radius r = mv⊥/(qB).
Faster particles make bigger circles but take the same time per revolution.

example.q: An electron moves at 4 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 9.1 × 10⁻⁴ T. Find the radius of its path. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

learn.reallife: Mass spectrometers at BARC, Mumbai, separate isotopes by bending ions in a magnetic field: heavier ions of the same charge and speed curve along larger radii.

games.title: Circling charges
items: The period of a charge circling in a uniform B depends on its speed.
T = 2πm/(qB) has no v.
Doubling the speed doubles the radius.
r ∝ v.
A charge entering at an angle to B follows a helix.
v∥ is unchanged while v⊥ circles.
The kinetic energy of the circling charge increases each revolution.
Magnetic force does no work.
A heavier ion with the same charge and speed moves on a larger circle.
r ∝ m.

quiz.q: A proton (m = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.1 T. What is the radius of its circular path (in cm)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: The speed of a charged particle moving in a circle in a uniform magnetic field is doubled. Its period of revolution
quiz.mistake: Thinks a faster particle must finish the circle sooner

quiz.q: A charged particle moving in a circle in a field B has radius 4 cm. If B is doubled (same speed), the radius becomes (in cm)
quiz.mistake: Thinks r increases with B

quiz.q: A particle with v∥ = 3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ along B has a period of 2 × 10⁻⁶ s for its circular part. What is the pitch of its helix (in m)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the perpendicular component instead of the parallel one

quiz.q: Which expression gives the angular frequency of a charge in a uniform magnetic field?
quiz.explain: From qvB = mω²r and v = ωr: ω = qB/m.
quiz.mistake: Writes the radius formula instead

quiz.q: An alpha particle (charge 2e, mass 4m) and a proton (charge e, mass m) enter the same field with the same speed, perpendicular to B. What is r(alpha)/r(proton)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the charge of the alpha particle

quiz.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at 60° to B. Its path will be
options: a helix with its axis along B
a circle in a plane containing B
quiz.explain: The component along B is unchanged; the perpendicular component gives circular motion. Together, a helix.
quiz.mistake: Applies the projectile (parabola) picture

quiz.q: An electron and a proton enter a uniform field perpendicularly with the same momentum. Which statement is correct?
options: The electron's circle is much bigger
The proton's circle is much bigger
They move on circles of the same radius but in opposite senses
quiz.explain: r = p/(qB) is the same for equal p and |q|, but opposite charges curve in opposite directions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the lighter particle always curves more

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a charge goes faster in a magnetic field, does it go round quicker?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Faster means a bigger circle, but the period 2πm/(qB) stays the same. Tricky!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the radius and the period depend on speed?

learn.hook: Coulomb's law gives the field of a point charge. For magnetism there are no magnetic charges, so Biot and Savart built the field from tiny pieces of current instead.
points: Biot-Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r/r³, magnitude dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r², where θ is between dl and r.
µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space), so µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
Similarities with Coulomb's law: both are inverse-square and long-range, and both obey superposition.
Differences: the source is a vector (I dl) not a scalar charge; dB depends on the angle θ and is perpendicular to both dl and r; dB = 0 along the line of the element.
Remarkably, µ₀ε₀ = 1/c², so c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

example.q: An element dl = 1 cm carrying 10 A lies along x. Find dB at 0.5 m along y from it.

learn.reallife: Engineers designing MRI machines for Indian hospitals compute the field of every turn of the coils by adding Biot-Savart contributions from tiny current elements.

games.title: Coulomb, Biot-Savart or both?
items: Inverse-square dependence
Source is a scalar charge
Source is a vector element I dl
Field depends on angle sinθ
Superposition holds
Field along the line joining source and point

items.text: dB is zero along the ___ of the current element.
dB depends on I dl sinθ divided by ___.

quiz.q: A current element of 2 A and length 5 mm is perpendicular to the line joining it to a point 10 cm away. What is dB at that point (in µT)?
quiz.mistake: Uses r instead of r²

quiz.q: For the same element (2 A, 5 mm), what is dB at a point 10 cm away along the line of the element (in µT)?
quiz.explain: θ = 0 along the element, and sin 0 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sinθ factor

quiz.q: What is the value of µ₀/4π in SI units?
quiz.mistake: Gives µ₀ itself or the electrostatic constant

quiz.q: In the Biot-Savart law, the direction of dB is
options: perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r
quiz.explain: dB ∝ dl × r, so it is perpendicular to both.
quiz.mistake: Thinks B points along r as E does

quiz.q: Which is a key difference between the Biot-Savart law and Coulomb's law?
options: The magnetic field depends on the angle between the current element and the position vector
Only the Biot-Savart law obeys superposition
Coulomb's law depends on a vector source
quiz.explain: The sinθ factor and the vector source I dl are unique to Biot-Savart.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the distance dependence differs

quiz.q: Using µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the value of 1/√(µ₀ε₀) is close to
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root

quiz.q: A current element at the origin points along +x. What is the direction of dB at a point on the +y axis?
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the cross product

quiz.q: A current element produces dB at a distance r. What is dB at 2r in the same direction (θ unchanged)?
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/r

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a tiny bit of current wire make a magnetic field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! By the Biot-Savart law, dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r². Add all the bits to get the full field!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law gives the field of a small current element, and how does it depend on angle and distance?

topics.title: Field of a circular current loop

learn.hook: Coil a wire into a loop and the field at its centre gets concentrated. Wind many loops and you have the coils of motors, speakers and MRI scanners.
points: On the axis of a loop of radius R at distance x from the centre: B = µ₀IR²/[2(x² + R²)^(3/2)], along the axis (from Biot-Savart; the perpendicular parts cancel by symmetry).
At the centre (x = 0): B = µ₀I/(2R). For N turns: B = µ₀NI/(2R).
For an arc subtending angle θ (in radians) at its centre: B = µ₀Iθ/(4πR). A semicircle gives µ₀I/(4R).
Right-hand thumb rule for a loop: curl the fingers along the current, and the thumb points along B through the loop.
Field lines of a loop are like those of a short bar magnet: they come out of one face and go into the other.

example.q: A coil of 200 turns, radius 8 cm, carries 0.5 A. Find B at its centre. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: The tangent galvanometer, once common in Indian college labs, uses the field at the centre of a circular coil, µ₀NI/2R, balanced against Earth's horizontal field.

games.title: Loop logic
items: At the centre of a loop, the field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop.
It is along the axis.
The field on the axis of a loop increases as you move away from the centre.
It is largest at the centre and falls with x.
Viewed from one side, a counter-clockwise current produces a field pointing towards the viewer.
Right-hand thumb rule.
Doubling the radius of a loop (same current) doubles the field at its centre.
B ∝ 1/R, so it halves.
A current loop's field lines resemble those of a bar magnet.
A loop is a magnetic dipole.

quiz.q: A single circular loop of radius 6.28 cm carries 10 A. What is the field at its centre (in µT)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 in the denominator

quiz.q: A coil of 50 turns and radius 3.14 cm carries 2 A. What is B at its centre (in mT)? (π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by N

quiz.q: A semicircular wire of radius 5 cm carries 4 A. What is the field at its centre (in µT)? (π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Uses the full-loop formula µ₀I/2R

quiz.q: The field at the centre of a loop is B. The same wire is bent into a loop of half the radius with 2 turns, carrying the same current. The new field at the centre is
quiz.explain: N doubles and R halves: B ∝ N/R gives 2/(1/2) = 4.
quiz.mistake: Considers only one of the two changes

quiz.q: On the axis of a loop of radius R, at a distance x = R from the centre, the field compared with the centre value B₀ is
quiz.mistake: Uses the inverse-square law along the axis

quiz.q: Why do the field components perpendicular to the axis cancel for a circular loop?
options: Elements on opposite ends of a diameter give equal and opposite perpendicular components
The field is zero everywhere off the axis
The current is zero in half the loop
Only the axial component exists for any wire
quiz.explain: By symmetry, the perpendicular components from diametrically opposite elements cancel in pairs.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the symmetry argument

quiz.q: A loop lies in the plane of the page with current flowing clockwise as you look at it. The field at its centre points
quiz.explain: Curl right-hand fingers clockwise: the thumb points into the page.
quiz.mistake: Uses the left hand

quiz.q: A quarter-circle arc of radius R carries current I. What is B at its centre?
quiz.mistake: Uses the semicircle result

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the direction of the magnetic field inside a current loop?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Curl the right-hand fingers along the current and the thumb points along B through the loop. Easy!
teach.nudge: Good! Which hand rule do we use, and what do the fingers and thumb represent?

topics.title: Ampere's circuital law and the straight wire

learn.hook: Gauss's law makes symmetric electric problems easy. Ampere's law does the same for magnetic fields of straight wires, cylinders and solenoids.
points: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = µ₀I, where I is the net current passing through the closed loop (the Amperian loop).
Choose a loop where B is constant and tangent (or normal, so B·dl = 0) by symmetry, just as a Gaussian surface is chosen for Gauss's law.
Long straight wire: a circle of radius r gives B(2πr) = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ I/r.
Direction: right-hand thumb rule. Thumb along the current, curled fingers give the circular field lines.
Long solid cylinder of radius a with uniform current I: outside B = µ₀I/(2πr); inside B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²), rising linearly from zero at the axis.

example.q: A long straight wire carries 5 A. Find B at 10 cm.
example.answer: 1 × 10⁻⁵ T, in circles around the wire

learn.reallife: Near a 765 kV transmission line carrying about 1000 A, the field 20 m below is about 10 µT, roughly a fifth of Earth's field. This is what B = µ₀I/(2πr) predicts.

games.title: Ampere's law for a straight wire
items: Note the field lines are circles around the wire
Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r
B is constant and tangent along the loop
∮B·dl = B × 2πr
Set equal to µ₀I and solve: B = µ₀I/(2πr)

games.title: Ampere's law check
items: Ampere's law relates the line integral of B to the current enclosed by the loop.
∮B·dl = µ₀I_enc.
The field of a long straight wire falls as 1/r².
It falls as 1/r.
Inside a long uniform cylindrical conductor, B increases linearly with distance from the axis.
B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²).
Currents outside the Amperian loop contribute to the enclosed current.
Only currents through the loop count.
The field at the axis of a long cylindrical conductor is zero.
No current is enclosed at r = 0.

quiz.q: A long straight wire carries 10 A. What is the magnetic field 5 cm from it (in µT)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 in µ₀/2π

quiz.q: The field 2 cm from a long wire is 60 µT. What is the field 6 cm from it (in µT)?
quiz.explain: B ∝ 1/r, so tripling r gives 60/3 = 20 µT.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/r²

quiz.q: A long wire carries current vertically upward. Viewed from above, the field lines around it are
quiz.explain: Point the right thumb up: fingers curl counter-clockwise as seen from above.
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule with the left hand

quiz.q: A long solid cylinder of radius 2 cm carries 4 A uniformly. What is B at 1 cm from the axis (in µT)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the outside formula µ₀I/(2πr)

quiz.q: For the same cylinder (4 A, radius 2 cm), what is B at 4 cm from the axis (in µT)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the inside formula outside

quiz.q: Ampere's circuital law states that ∮B·dl equals
options: µ₀ times the total current anywhere
µ₀ times the net current through the loop
quiz.explain: Only current crossing the surface bounded by the loop counts.
quiz.mistake: Includes currents outside the loop

quiz.q: Two long wires pass through a closed loop: one carries 3 A upward and the other 5 A downward. A third wire, outside the loop, carries 10 A upward. Taking upward as positive, what is ∮B·dl in units of µ₀ (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Includes the 10 A outside

quiz.q: Ampere's law plays the same role for magnetic fields that which law plays for electric fields?
quiz.explain: Both use symmetry with a chosen surface or loop to find fields simply.
quiz.mistake: Pairs it with Coulomb's law

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I find the magnetic field of a long wire without adding up every tiny bit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Use Ampere's law with a circular loop: B × 2πr = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/2πr. Symmetry saves the day!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law and which shape of loop make this easy?

learn.hook: Wind a wire tightly into a long coil and you can create a strong, uniform magnetic field inside, a magnet you can switch on and off.
points: A long solenoid has a nearly uniform field inside along its axis, and a nearly zero field outside.
Ampere's law with a rectangular loop (one side inside, one outside) gives BL = µ₀(nL)I, so B = µ₀nI, where n = N/L is turns per unit length.
B inside does not depend on the radius or the exact position inside (for a long solenoid).
The solenoid's field resembles a bar magnet's: one end acts as a north pole, the other as a south pole. Use the right-hand rule to find which end is north.
At each end of a long solenoid the field is about half the value inside, µ₀nI/2.

learn.hook: Two parallel wires both carrying current towards the same end pull towards each other. That tiny tug was once the official definition of the ampere.
points: Wire a creates B = µ₀Ia/(2πd) at wire b. Force per unit length on b: f = µ₀IaIb/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ IaIb/d.
Currents in the same direction (parallel) attract; currents in opposite directions (antiparallel) repel. This is opposite to the rule for like charges.
The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite (Newton's third law).
Historical definition (used until 2019): one ampere is the current which, in two long straight parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length.
Since 2019, the ampere is defined by fixing the value of the elementary charge e.

example.q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 8 A in the same direction. Find the force per metre.

learn.reallife: In large power stations and substations, bus bars carrying thousands of amperes are clamped firmly because the force between parallel currents can bend them during a short-circuit surge.

learn.hook: Put a current loop in a magnetic field and it twists. That twist turns the shaft of every DC motor and the needle of every analogue meter.
points: Rectangular loop in a uniform field: the forces on opposite sides cancel, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple.
Torque τ = IAB sinθ for one turn, where θ is between the normal to the loop and B. For N turns: τ = NIAB sinθ.
Vector form: τ = m × B, where the magnetic moment m = NIA (unit A m²), directed along the normal by the right-hand rule.
Stable equilibrium when m is parallel to B (θ = 0); unstable when m is antiparallel (θ = 180°). Torque is zero in both.
Torque is maximum (NIAB) when the plane of the loop is parallel to B (θ = 90°).

example.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.01 m² carries 2 A in a 0.5 T field, with its plane parallel to B. Find the torque.
steps: Plane parallel to B means θ = 90° between normal and B

learn.reallife: The small DC motors in battery-powered toy cars, cordless drills and car windscreen wipers rely on τ = NIAB sinθ to turn their coils.

topics.title: A current loop as a magnetic dipole

learn.hook: A tiny current loop behaves exactly like a tiny bar magnet. In fact, the magnetism of atoms comes from electrons looping around nuclei.
points: Far along the axis (x ≫ R), a loop's field is B = µ₀m/(2πx³) = (µ₀/4π)(2m/x³), where m = IA.
Compare the electric dipole: E = (1/4πε₀)(2p/x³). Swap p → m and 1/ε₀ → µ₀.
A current loop is a magnetic dipole, with north and south faces.
Unlike electric charges, there are no isolated magnetic charges (monopoles): the simplest magnetic element is the current loop (dipole).
Problem toolkit: B of wires, loops and solenoids; force on wires; torque NIAB sinθ; radius mv/(qB).

example.q: A loop of area 0.01 m² carries 1 A. Find the axial field 1 m away.

learn.reallife: The hard disk drives in Indian data centres store bits as tiny magnetic regions that behave like small magnetic dipoles, each arising from aligned atomic current loops.

learn.hook: The swinging needle of an old-school analogue meter is a coil, a magnet and a tiny spring working together, a beautiful use of τ = NIAB.
points: Construction: a coil of N turns on a soft iron core, pivoted between concave pole pieces of a permanent magnet, which make the field radial so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B.
Magnetic torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ: kφ = NIAB, so φ = (NAB/k)I. Deflection is proportional to current, giving a linear scale.
Current sensitivity = φ/I = NAB/k (deflection per unit current).
Voltage sensitivity = φ/V = NAB/(kR), where R is the coil resistance.
Doubling N doubles the current sensitivity, but it also doubles R, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same.

example.q: A galvanometer coil has N = 100, A = 2 × 10⁻³ m², B = 0.5 T, k = 10⁻⁴ N m rad⁻¹. Find the current sensitivity.
example.answer: 1000 rad per ampere (1 rad per mA)

learn.reallife: School physics labs across India still use moving coil galvanometers to find null points in bridge experiments, because they respond to very small currents.

topics.title: Converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter

learn.hook: A galvanometer is delicate, often going full scale at a few milliamperes. With one well-chosen resistor it becomes a sturdy ammeter or a voltmeter.
points: Ammeter: connect a small shunt resistance S in parallel with the galvanometer (resistance G). Most current bypasses the coil.
Shunt value: S = IgG/(I - Ig), where Ig is the full-scale galvanometer current and I is the required range. The ammeter's resistance is very low, about S.
Voltmeter: connect a large resistance R in series with the galvanometer.
Series value: R = V/Ig - G for a voltmeter of range V. The voltmeter's total resistance is very high.
An ideal ammeter has zero resistance (connected in series); an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance (connected in parallel).

example.q: A galvanometer of G = 99 Ω gives full deflection at 1 mA. Find the shunt for a 0–100 mA ammeter.

learn.reallife: Multimeters sold in Delhi's Lajpat Rai Market switch between ranges by connecting different shunts and series resistors to the same sensitive meter movement.
